findings.consequence: The new `optimized_pagination=true` mode returns HTTP 500 on the audit-log endpoint for admins. Crafted cursors with a negative offset also raise a server error.
findings.explanation: The audit log endpoint orders by "-datetime" and, when `optimized_pagination=true` and the user is an admin, now paginates with OptimizedCursorPaginator. That class extends BasePaginator directly, not DateTimePaginator. Its get_item_key calls math.floor/ceil on the raw `datetime` attribute, which raises TypeError for datetime objects. Its value_from_cursor returns the raw numeric cursor value instead of converting a timestamp to a datetime, so the queryset filter built from a cursor gets a number where a datetime is expected. Any request with a non-empty result set reaches build_cursor with key=get_item_key and fails. Separately, the `enable_advanced_features` branch slices the queryset with a negative start (`queryset[cursor.offset:stop]`). Django querysets reject negative indexing with an AssertionError, and Cursor.from_string accepts negative offsets from user input, so a crafted cur…

findings.consequence: A request to the audit log endpoint with `optimized_pagination=true` and a negative cursor offset fails with an unhandled assertion, which returns a 500. The new paginator does not deliver the negative-offset pagination it advertises.
findings.explanation: When `enable_advanced_features` is set and `cursor.offset < 0`, `get_result` runs `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with `start_offset = cursor.offset`. The comment claims the Django ORM handles negative slicing. It does not: Django querysets raise `AssertionError: Negative indexing is not supported.` The audit log endpoint passes `enable_advanced_features=True` for superusers and global-access members who send `optimized_pagination=true`. The cursor offset comes from the user-supplied `cursor` query parameter, so a cursor such as `0:-5:0` reaches this branch. The change to `BasePaginator.get_result` is not a bug. It clamps negative non-prev offsets to 0 and leaves prev offsets unchanged. The comment there about negative offsets is misleading, but it is only a comment.
findings.title: Negative-offset branch slices a Django queryset with a negative index, which raises

findings.consequence: Stats requests for allowlisted projects can fail with an invalid-search-query or Snuba unknown-column error. When the query does run, `sum(sample_weight)` can be wrong if the column is missing or null. Ordinary error charts, dashboards and alerts for those projects stop working.
findings.explanation: For allowlisted projects, `_get_event_stats` rewrites `count()` to `upsampled_count() as count` and passes it to the timeseries, top-events and RPC query paths. `upsampled_count` is defined only in `DiscoverDatasetConfig` (discover.py:1041-1052), and it sums a `sample_weight` column. The rest of `src/sentry` has no definition of that column or that function. The errors dataset and the RPC datasets (`use_rpc`) use their own resolvers, so they have no `upsampled_count` function to resolve. The rewrite also passes the alias `as count` to every path, including the top-events path. Its eligibility gate, `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects`, returns True for `dataset == errors` and for any discover query whose text contains `event.type:error`. A request to events-stats with `yAxis=count()` for an allowlisted project is therefore rewritten to a function or column the backend cannot r…
findings.title: Upsampling rewrites count() to upsampled_count(), which most query paths cannot resolve

findings.consequence: For allowlisted projects, error counts in the events-stats endpoint are undercounted. They can be zero for any time range that contains events without sample_weight.
findings.explanation: transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling replaces count() with upsampled_count(), which is toInt64(sum(sample_weight)). The code assumes every event in an allowlisted project has sample_weight, but nothing enforces this. The only writer in the diff is a test factory helper. Events stored before the project was allowlisted, or events from SDKs that send no client_sample_rate, have NULL or 0 sample_weight, and sum ignores NULLs. Those events therefore contribute 0 instead of 1. Separately, the eligibility cache (60s) has invalidate_upsampling_cache defined but nothing calls it, so allowlist changes are not applied immediately.
findings.title: count() rewritten to sum(sample_weight) with no fallback for events lacking sample_weight

findings.consequence: Error events can be labelled with the wrong `id`. The `id` is not used in the log message, so this is a minor data-integrity issue.
findings.explanation: `nodestore.backend.get_multi` returns a dict keyed by node ID, and it may omit missing nodes. `events.values()` is zipped positionally with `error_ids`. If any node is missing, or the dict order differs from the input order, the IDs shift onto the wrong events. The `if data is not None` filter only helps if missing nodes are present as None entries.
findings.title: zip(error_ids, events.values()) can pair error IDs with the wrong events

findings.consequence: Each page's summary includes errors that did not occur in that page's time window. Errors are duplicated across pages and placed out of chronological order. The summaries are misleading, and the Seer request payloads are larger than they need to be.
findings.explanation: `get()` fetches the replay's error events once. It passes the whole list to every page through `functools.partial(analyze_recording_segments, error_events)`. `paginate` calls `on_results` once per page of segments, and each call goes through `gen_request_data`. That function ends with a loop (lines 165-168) that emits every error not yet emitted. The error list is not consumed across pages, so each page's request to Seer gets its own copy of the errors. Errors timestamped after the page's last event are emitted at the end of every page. Errors that fall between events are emitted on the first page that has a later event. Pages that do not contain an error's real position also get it. For example, a replay with 3 pages and 2 errors sends both errors to Seer on all 3 pages.
findings.title: Error log lines are repeated on every page of the paginated summary

findings.consequence: All errors are emitted before the first breadcrumb instead of at their chronological position, so the interleaving the code claims to provide does not happen. I did not check whether `as_log_message` normalizes timestamps.
findings.explanation: Nodestore event `timestamp` is a float in epoch seconds, about 1.7e9. Replay recording events carry millisecond timestamps, about 1.7e12. The check `error_events[error_idx]["timestamp"] < event.get("timestamp", 0)` is therefore true for every error against the first event with a timestamp.
findings.title: Error timestamps (seconds) are compared with replay event timestamps (milliseconds)

findings.consequence: In the default view with no search text, the attributes that should be hidden still appear in the span attributes list. They disappear only after the user starts searching, so the behaviour is inconsistent.

When `searchQuery` is empty, the memo returns early with `return sorted` (lines 61-63) and never reaches that filter. So `is_segment`, `project_id` and `received` are shown by default and are only hidden once the user types a search query. That is the opposite of the intent of a hidden-attributes list.

findings.consequence: After a hang, two flusher processes can flush the same shards at once. That can produce duplicate segments on Kafka. The leaked hung process also keeps its Redis and Kafka resources and is never cleaned up. On shutdown, the child processes are not terminated.
findings.explanation: The processes are created from `multiprocessing.get_context("spawn").Process`, which is `SpawnProcess`. `SpawnProcess` subclasses `BaseProcess`. It does not subclass `multiprocessing.Process`, which is `multiprocessing.context.Process`. So `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` at line 254 is False for real spawned processes, and `process.kill()` is skipped. The old code called `self.process.kill()` unconditionally. When the cause is "hang", the process is still alive. The code then calls `_create_process_for_shards`, which starts a second process for the same shards and overwrites `self.processes[process_index]`. The hung process is never killed and is no longer tracked. The same check in `join` (line 346) skips `terminate()` for the same reason.
findings.title: Hung flusher processes are never killed because isinstance check uses the wrong Process class

findings.consequence: Flusher processes can keep running after the consumer strategy is joined, for example during rebalance or shutdown. They may keep flushing and producing to Kafka after the strategy is gone. They are only reaped when the parent exits, because they are daemon processes.
findings.explanation: The old join() always called terminate() on the single flusher process after its wait loop, even when the timeout had expired. The new loop breaks out when the deadline is reached (line 341). The terminate() call sits at the end of the loop body, so it never runs for the current process or any later one. Example: timeout=5 and 3 flusher processes. The first process hangs for the full 5s, so the second and third hit the break and are never terminated.
findings.title: join() skips terminate() for remaining flusher processes once the deadline passes

findings.consequence: The added wait does nothing, so test_basic stays timing-dependent and can fail intermittently. The change gives a false impression of a fix.
findings.explanation: test_basic starts with monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None). The added `time.sleep(0.1)` resolves through the `time` module attribute, so it calls the no-op lambda and waits for nothing. The comment says it gives the flusher threads time to process after the drift change, but no waiting happens. The flusher runs in separate processes, so step.join() may run before the segment is flushed. The test then races on `(msg,) = messages`.
findings.title: Added time.sleep(0.1) in test_basic is a no-op because time.sleep is monkeypatched

findings.consequence: The issue event's monitor context shows the raw schedule_type value and not the readable one the code meant to send. The dead copy also hides the mistake.
findings.explanation: get_monitor_environment_context copies monitor.config into `config`. It then replaces `schedule_type` in that copy with the display string. The returned dict uses `monitor_environment.monitor.config` for the "config" key, not the local `config`, so the copy and its substitution are never used. findings.consequence: After each restart or rebalance, the last processed message per partition is processed again, which duplicates subscription results. Partitions with offset gaps stop committing, so large amounts of data are replayed after a restart.
findings.explanation: get_committable_offsets returns the highest processed offset (highest_committable), and _commit_loop passes it unchanged to commit_function (line 287). Arroyo's commit callback expects the next offset to consume (message.committable is offset+1). So after processing offset N, N is committed and the consumer resumes at N, reprocessing the last message of every partition after a restart or rebalance. Separately, the scan breaks at the first offset not in all_offsets. Real Kafka topics can have offset gaps (compaction, transaction markers). A gap makes the partition's commit stall permanently at the gap.
findings.title: Commits last processed offset instead of next offset, and stalls on offset gaps

findings.consequence: On a graceful close, messages already accepted into the queues are silently dropped, and completed work is never committed. They are redelivered after restart, so processing is duplicated. This contradicts the "Gracefully shutdown" docstring and the "No item is lost" guarantee in the class docstring.
findings.explanation: FixedQueuePool.shutdown sets worker.shutdown = True and then calls q.shutdown(immediate=False), which is meant to let queued items drain. OrderedQueueWorker.run checks `while not self.shutdown` after each item. A worker therefore exits after its current item and abandons everything still queued. SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() stops the commit thread (with a 5s join) before the pool is shut down. Nothing commits the offsets that finish during or after shutdown. terminate() also does not join the commit thread.
findings.title: Shutdown sets worker flag so queued items are not drained, and no final commit occurs

findings.consequence: The test is flaky in CI and fails intermittently with no code defect behind it. To make it deterministic, block the processor on an event until after the stats assertions.
findings.explanation: In test_stats_reporting (line 199-200), 10 items are submitted to queues that have running worker threads. get_stats() sums qsize(), and a worker removes an item from its queue as soon as it calls get(). The processing callback is trivial. By the time the test thread calls get_stats(), the workers can already have taken every item, so total_items is 0 and `assert stats["total_items"] > 0` fails. Whether it fails depends on thread scheduling.
findings.title: test_stats_reporting asserts queue depth > 0 while workers are draining concurrently

findings.consequence: Rare intermittent failures in CI.
findings.explanation: test_offset_committing (line 285-300) and the offset-gap test wait on commit_event, which is set by the first commit call. The commit loop ticks every 1s from strategy construction. If a tick lands while the 5 items are still being processed, a partial offset such as 102 is committed. commit_event is then set, and the assertion `== 104` fails.
findings.title: test_offset_committing can see a partial commit

findings.consequence: Occasional CI failures with no code change. Because hash() is salted per process, consistent assignment is also only guaranteed within a single process, not across processes.
findings.explanation: FixedQueuePool.get_queue_for_group uses the built-in hash(group_key) % num_queues. For str, hash is salted per process unless PYTHONHASHSEED is fixed. test_different_groups_distributed asserts that 20 keys cover all 3 queues. With a random salt, the chance that some queue gets no key is about 3*(2/3)^20, roughly 0.1%, so the assertion fails on some runs. The same pattern applies to test_stats_reporting, which asserts total_items > 0 right after submitting. Workers are already consuming at that point, so that assertion is racy too.
findings.title: Distribution test depends on per-process randomized str hash and can flake

findings.consequence: The test is flaky under CPU contention in CI and can fail intermittently without any product defect.
findings.explanation: The test submits 10 items to a pool with live worker threads and then asserts stats["total_items"] > 0. total_items is the sum of qsize(), and qsize() drops as soon as a worker calls get(). The processor is trivial (it appends under a lock). If the workers drain all 10 items before the main thread calls get_stats() (for example after a GIL switch while submitting), total_items is 0 and the assertion fails.
findings.title: Racy assertion on queue depth in test_stats_reporting

findings.consequence: The test is flaky and gives false assurance. It contradicts its own docstring and the real behavior, where a failed item's offset is still committed. A regression in error handling would go unnoticed.
findings.explanation: The test's docstring says errors must not block offset commits. Its assertion at line 1922 requires that the partition is not committed. The worker (queue_consumer.py:148-149) calls complete_offset in a `finally`, so a failed item still counts as processed. After offsets 100 and 101 finish, get_committable_offsets returns 101 and the commit loop would commit 102. The assertion holds only because the commit thread first waits 1.0s (queue_consumer.py:276). The test loop breaks about 0.3s after both mock calls finish, so the assertion runs before the first commit. Nothing in the test pins this ordering. Under CI load, the loop can run longer, a commit can land first, and the test fails. On a normal run, it checks nothing about commits.
findings.title: Error-handling test asserts the opposite of the implementation and passes only by timing

findings.consequence: The test is timing-dependent and can fail intermittently on a slow machine. When it passes, it doesn't verify the behavior its docstring describes: that a failed message doesn't block commits of later messages. It also encodes a behavior (no commit after failure) that the implementation doesn't have.
findings.explanation: test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling expects that no offset is committed for the partition after the first message fails. OrderedQueueWorker.run calls complete_offset in a `finally` block, so a failed offset is still marked complete. get_committable_offsets then returns it, and the commit loop commits offset+1. The docstring says errors don't block commits for other messages. The assertion says the opposite. The test passes only because _commit_loop first waits 1.0s (shutdown_event.wait(1.0)). The test stops polling as soon as the queue is empty and the mock has been called twice, then sleeps 0.2s and asserts. If the commit loop fires inside that window, for example on a slow CI machine, the assertion fails. Even when it passes, it checks nothing about error handling.
findings.title: Error-handling test asserts no commit, contradicting the worker, and passes only through timing

findings.consequence: The test is timing-dependent and can be flaky. When it passes, it verifies nothing about commit behavior after a processing error. A regression where failed messages block or skip commits would go undetected. It also encodes a behavior (no commit) that the implementation does not have.
findings.explanation: The docstring of test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling says errors must not block offset commits. The worker's `finally` in OrderedQueueWorker.run always calls complete_offset, even when the processor raises. So once the 1s commit loop runs, offsets 100 and 101 are both complete and get_committable_offsets returns 101. commit_offsets then commits 102. The test asserts the opposite: `len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets` at line 1922. That assertion holds only because the wait loop exits about 0.3s after the queue drains. The SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy commit thread first commits after `shutdown_event.wait(1.0)`, which is later than that. If the test thread is delayed by more than a second, for example on a loaded CI machine, the commit lands first and the test fails. As written, it never checks the behavior it claims to check.
findings.title: Error-handling test asserts no commit, contradicting its docstring and the implementation, and passes only by timing

findings.explanation: trigger_refresh_routing_form_response_denormalized_booking is fired on UPDATE OF "userId" on Booking. It sets "bookingUserId" = NEW."userId" but never updates "bookingUserName", "bookingUserEmail" or "bookingUserAvatarUrl". Those columns are only refreshed by the users trigger, which fires on changes to the user row, and by the full refresh function. When a booking is reassigned to another host, the denormalized row therefore holds the new user id with the old user's name, email and avatar. Two related gaps exist. The booking INSERT trigger reuses this function and updates WHERE rfrd."bookingId" = NEW.id. A response written before its booking exists has a NULL bookingId, so no row matches and it is never linked to the booking. findings.consequence: On Linux, re-running the script when .env already has GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL leaves the stale URL in place. The script still prints "✅ Updated". A failed run also exits with status 0.
findings.explanation: The script updates an existing GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL with `sed -i '' -E ...`. That form works only with BSD/macOS sed. On GNU sed (Linux), the empty string is read as the script and the real expression is treated as a file name, so the replacement fails and the existing .env line is not updated. Separately, the failure paths (no tunnel URL, rate limit) call `cleanup`, which always runs `exit 0`, so callers can't tell that the script failed.

findings.consequence: A failed calendar or video event deletion during reschedule is no longer logged by the existing handler and surfaces as an unhandled rejection. That can crash the process on newer Node versions or fail silently, and the old event may be left on the calendar.
findings.explanation: The callback passed to forEach was changed to async so it can await getCalendar. forEach ignores the returned promise, so the surrounding try/catch (which logs errors) can no longer catch anything thrown inside the callback. This covers getCalendar, calendar.deleteEvent and deleteMeeting, and the same pattern appears in the bookings.tsx requestReschedule handler, which has no try/catch at all. Before the change, a synchronous throw from getCalendar was caught and logged. Now a rejection from getCalendar (for example a failed dynamic import of the app module) or from deleteEvent becomes an unhandled promise rejection. The reschedule flow also continues and returns before the deletions finish.

findings.consequence: A malformed request gets an unhandled 500 instead of a 400 IncorrectBackupCode. This is a low-impact robustness issue, and the caller is already authenticated.
findings.explanation: The new backup-code branch calls req.body.backupCode.replaceAll("-", "") without checking the type. The branch is entered whenever backupCode is truthy. A JSON body such as {"backupCode": 123} or {"backupCode": {}} makes replaceAll undefined or not a function, so the handler throws a TypeError. The other failure paths in this handler return a 400 with an ErrorCode. The hypothesis's other concerns do not hold. Backup codes are all cleared by the final update (backupCodes: null), so no code needs to be consumed separately. The password check that is skipped for non-CAL identity providers was already there before this change.
findings.title: Non-string backupCode crashes the handler with an unhandled TypeError

findings.consequence: A leaked or intercepted backup code can be used several times by parallel requests, and a code consumed by one login can be restored by a concurrent write. This weakens the single-use guarantee of the second factor.
findings.explanation: The authorize function reads user.backupCodes in the initial findUnique. It decrypts them and matches the supplied code with indexOf. It then sets the matched slot to null and writes the whole re-encrypted array back with prisma.user.update. Nothing is atomic: there is no transaction, no compare-and-set on the stored ciphertext, and no re-read before the write. Two concurrent logins with the same backup code both read the array while the code is still present. Both pass the indexOf check and both succeed. The second write also overwrites the first, and with different codes one login's consumption can be lost. This lets a single-use code authenticate more than once. Requests are limited only by the shared checkRateLimitAndThrowError, which is called before the backup code check. I could not read the limiter's configuration, so I did not assess it.
findings.title: Backup code consumption is a non-atomic read-modify-write, so one code can be replayed

findings.consequence: An attacker who knows only a victim's email can log in without the password. For a user with 2FA disabled, any totpCode value is enough. For a user with 2FA enabled, a single backup code is enough, because the password step is bypassed. Either path takes over the account.
findings.explanation: At line 121, `if (user.password && !credentials.totpCode)` verifies the password only when no totpCode is supplied. The same totpCode guard skips the identity-provider checks at lines 113 and 117. The new backup-code branch (line 131) is chosen whenever `twoFactorEnabled && backupCode`. It never checks the password and never reads totpCode. A request with {email, backupCode: <valid>, totpCode: "x"} therefore skips the password check and succeeds on the backup code alone. If twoFactorEnabled is false, {email, totpCode: "x"} skips the password check and no second-factor branch runs (line 157 is not entered). authorize() then returns the user with no credential verified. verifyPassword is never reached in either case.
findings.title: Password check skipped whenever totpCode is present, so the new backup-code login needs no password

prs.title: feat: 2fa backup codes

findings.consequence: When the caller passes no externalCalendarId, deleting a Google event targets the user's primary calendar instead of the booking's destination calendar, so the event is not found or not removed. Updating an event with no calendarId fails the API call.
findings.explanation: The fallback branch only runs when externalCalendarId is falsy, but it searches destinationCalendar for an entry whose externalId === externalCalendarId. That compares against a falsy value, so it never matches a real calendar and the result is undefined. The old code fell back to destinationCalendar.externalId. In deleteEvent (line 317) the calendarId then becomes "primary". In updateEvent (line 256) selectedCalendar is undefined, so events.update gets no calendarId.
findings.title: Google deleteEvent/updateEvent lose destination calendar fallback when externalCalendarId is empty

findings.consequence: Google events.update is called without a calendarId when the caller omits externalCalendarId.
findings.explanation: This is the same defect in updateEvent. When externalCalendarId is falsy, the lookup compares each cal.externalId to that falsy value and returns undefined, so selectedCalendar is undefined. The old code used destinationCalendar.externalId.
findings.title: updateEvent fallback calendar lookup is always undefined

findings.consequence: Creating a Google Meet booking for a host with no destination calendar throws a TypeError in `EventManager.create`. The booking creation or confirmation fails. Before this change, the code fell back to Cal Video.
findings.explanation: The change makes `destinationCalendar` an array. The callers in confirm.handler, editLocation.handler and bookingReminder now pass `[]` when neither the booking nor the user has a destination calendar. `EventManager.create` runs `const [mainHostDestinationCalendar] = evt.destinationCalendar ?? [];`, which is `undefined` for an empty array or a missing value. The next line then reads `mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration` with no optional chaining. The old code used `evt.destinationCalendar?.integration`, which was safe. For any event whose location is Google Meet and which has no destination calendar, this throws a TypeError.
findings.title: Meet fallback dereferences undefined when destinationCalendar is an empty array

findings.consequence: The event is not created on those team members' destination calendars. Booking-level destinationCalendar is also left unset.
findings.explanation: evt.destinationCalendar is set to null when neither eventType.destinationCalendar nor organizerUser.destinationCalendar exists. The following `evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...teamDestinationCalendars)` is then a silent no-op, so the destination calendars collected from the other COLLECTIVE hosts are discarded. Failing case: a collective event where the organizer has no destination calendar but another host does. The array is null and that host's calendar is never used.
findings.title: Collective team members' destination calendars dropped when organizer/event type has none

findings.consequence: On instances with team billing disabled, newly created organizations have no slug and no requestedSlug. The org subdomain and its routing are then broken, and the slug cannot be recovered from metadata.
findings.explanation: The old code was `...(!IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED && { slug })`, which set the slug when billing was disabled. The change rewrote it as `IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED ? { slug } : {}` and dropped the negation. The slug is now set only when billing is enabled, which is the opposite of before. That is also the only case where `requestedSlug` is stored. When billing is enabled, the org gets its slug immediately, and the pending-slug flow in `requestedSlug` is no longer a separate step. When billing is disabled (the self-hosted default), the org is created with neither `slug` nor `requestedSlug`.
findings.title: Organization slug condition inverted: slug only set when team billing is enabled

prs.title: fix: handle collective multiple host on destinationCalendar
feat: convert InsightsBookingService to use Prisma.sql raw queries

findings.consequence: On serverless runtimes the response can end before the cancellation requests finish. Old reminders for a rescheduled or cancelled booking may then still be sent, or the reminder rows may not be deleted or marked cancelled. Failures are only logged to the console.
findings.explanation: deleteScheduledEmailReminder and deleteScheduledSMSReminder are async functions: they call prisma and SendGrid/Twilio. In handleNewBooking.ts lines 966-972 the calls are fired inside forEach with no await. The surrounding try/catch therefore catches nothing, because the functions swallow their own errors. The reschedule flow continues without waiting for the cancellations. handleCancelBooking.ts has the same problem. The old code put the DB deletes in Promise.all. The new code calls the helpers unawaited, after which it only awaits the attendee and booking-reference deletes and then returns. The helpers also behave differently from the old code. For email with immediateDelete=true, the reminder row is never removed or marked cancelled after the batch is cancelled at SendGrid.
findings.title: Async reminder deletions are not awaited, so the try/catch is ineffective and work can be lost

findings.consequence: If the key is missing, cancelled or rescheduled bookings are never cancelled in SendGrid and the reminder emails are still sent. The reminder rows are not deleted, so the cron retries and fails on every run.
findings.explanation: The file calls only `sgMail.setApiKey(sendgridAPIKey)` at line 19. It then uses the separate `@sendgrid/client` singleton in `client.request` at lines 57 and 188, to cancel scheduled sends and to create a batch id. The only `client.setApiKey` calls in the repo are in `emailReminderManager.ts:26` and `Sendgrid.ts:57`. This file does not import `emailReminderManager.ts`. `Sendgrid.ts` sets the key only inside a constructor. If this cron route runs in a process that has not loaded `emailReminderManager`, the client has no Authorization header and SendGrid answers 401. The cancel loop is wrapped in a try/catch that only logs the error, so the failure is hidden. I did not check whether some other module on the route's import path loads `emailReminderManager`, so this depends on how Next.js bundles the route.
findings.title: @sendgrid/client never receives an API key in the reminder cron handler

findings.consequence: One cancelled SMS reminder, or any reminder with a null or invalid `referenceId`, can stop email cancellations for the whole batch. Scheduled emails for cancelled or rescheduled bookings may then still be sent. Non-email reminder rows can also be deleted by the email cron.
findings.explanation: The `remindersToCancel` query filters only on `cancelled: true` and `scheduledDate`. The other queries in this handler filter on `method: WorkflowMethods.EMAIL`. Cancelled SMS or WhatsApp reminders due within the next hour are therefore picked up too. Each one is sent to SendGrid's `/v3/user/scheduled_sends` with its `referenceId` as `batch_id`. That id is not a SendGrid batch id, and may be null. SendGrid is likely to reject the request, and `client.request` then throws. The `catch` is outside the `for` loop, so the first failure ends the loop and every remaining reminder is skipped, including valid email ones. The `prisma.workflowReminder.delete` calls are lazy and only run at `Promise.all` after the loop. A throw therefore skips every delete, including those for reminders SendGrid has already cancelled. Those reminders are retried on the next run. If the request does succeed for a no…
findings.title: Cancel query lacks method filter, so non-email reminders go to SendGrid and are deleted

findings.consequence: One bad or already-cancelled batch id can stall all cancellations in this cron run, and in every later run. Cancelled reminders after it in the list are not cancelled in SendGrid. Emails for cancelled or rescheduled bookings can still be sent, and the cancelled rows are never cleaned up.
findings.explanation: In the new cancel block of the cron handler, `prisma.workflowReminder.delete(...)` returns a lazy PrismaPromise. It only runs when awaited, and `Promise.all` is reached only after the whole `for` loop finishes. Each reminder is first cancelled in SendGrid with `await client.request(...)` inside a single `try`. If that call throws for one reminder, the `catch` logs the error and the loop ends. The deletes queued for earlier reminders are never run, and later reminders are never processed. The rows stay `cancelled: true` and match the `findMany` again on every run. Cancelling a batch SendGrid has already cancelled can itself return an error, so the same early reminder fails again on the next run. That reminder then blocks everything behind it in the list. I did not verify SendGrid's response to a repeat cancel.
findings.title: Cron cancel loop aborts on first SendGrid error, skips DB deletes and retries forever

prs.title: Comprehensive workflow reminder management for booking lifecycle events

findings.consequence: Slots that overrun the end of the host's working hours are reported as available and can be booked.
findings.explanation: In checkIfIsAvailable, `end` is computed with the same expression as `start` (slotStartTime hour*60+minute) instead of using slotEndTime. The `end > workingHour.endTime` test therefore only looks at the slot's start. A slot that starts inside working hours but runs past workingHour.endTime (for example a 60-minute slot starting 16:30 with hours ending 17:00) is not rejected. A second, smaller defect is in the same block: the `dayjs(...).add(...) === dayjs(...).add(...)` comparison compares object references and is always false, so the zero-length override branch is dead code.
findings.title: Working-hours check computes `end` from the slot start, so slot end is never checked

prs.title: Advanced date override handling and timezone compatibility improvements

findings.consequence: A timing side channel on the shared secret is possible in principle. It is hard to exploit over a network, which is why this is low severity. Authenticated callers who send malformed input get an unhandled 500.
findings.explanation: The handler compares the request header to process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET with `!==`, which is not constant-time. The unset-secret bypass in the hypothesis does not occur. APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED in packages/lib/constants.ts:103 is truthy only when both CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET and CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY are non-empty, and the handler returns 403 before the comparison when it is falsy. The `|| ""` fallback on the encryption key is therefore unreachable. A separate issue: `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse` and `JSON.parse` are not wrapped in try/catch, so a malformed body or a bad ciphertext throws and returns a 500 instead of a 400.
findings.title: Webhook secret compared with non-constant-time !==

findings.consequence: With credential sharing enabled, every refreshed credential is saved without an expiry. isExpired then treats it as expired, so a refresh and a call to the sync endpoint happen on every request. The stored refresh_token is also replaced by the dummy string. Validation of the expiry field is effectively absent.
findings.explanation: The computed keys `[z.string().toString()]` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]` both evaluate to the literal string "[object Object]", not a wildcard. The second overrides the first, so the schema is `{access_token, "[object Object]"?: unknown}`. Zod's default object parsing strips unknown keys, so a sync-endpoint response like `{access_token, expiry_date}` or `{access_token, expires_in}` is parsed to `{access_token}` only. The intended "any numeric property is the expiry" check is not enforced. parseRefreshTokenResponse then adds the placeholder refresh_token "refresh_token". Callers such as office365calendar merge `tokenResponse.data` into the stored credential, so the real refresh_token is overwritten by the placeholder and no expiry value is stored.
findings.title: minimumTokenResponseSchema uses bogus computed keys and strips expiry fields

findings.consequence: With credential sync enabled, the first refresh corrupts the saved refresh_token in the database. Later refreshes fail because the refresh token is invalid. The expiry is never updated, so every call triggers a refresh. Integrations that persist the parsed data, such as Office365, are affected.
findings.explanation: The two computed keys, z.string().toString() and z.string().optional().toString(), both evaluate to the same constant, "[object Object]". Zod does not override toString. The second key overwrites the first, so the schema is really {access_token: string, "[object Object]": unknown.optional()}. The "any number property is the expiry" rule is never enforced. The default z.object strips unknown keys, so the parsed data holds only access_token. It loses expiry_date, expires_in, refresh_token and any other fields. The hypothesis that safeParse always fails is wrong. The schema accepts any object with a string access_token, but it drops everything else. parseRefreshTokenResponse then sets data.refresh_token to the literal "refresh_token" because the stripped data never has one. Callers merge this data into the stored credential. For example, office365calendar/lib/CalendarService.ts:264 spreads…
findings.title: Credential-sync token schema is degenerate and placeholder refresh_token overwrites stored credentials

findings.consequence: After the first access-token refresh, a user's Google Calendar credential is overwritten with a malformed key. Every later use of that credential fails, and the user has to reconnect.
findings.explanation: parseRefreshTokenResponse returns the zod safeParse result, which has the shape {success, data}. It does not return the parsed data. The old code stored `googleCredentialSchema.parse(googleCredentials)`, which was the credential itself. The new code assigns the wrapper to `key` and passes it to prisma.credential.update. After the first token refresh, the stored key is {success: true, data: {...}}. It no longer has access_token, refresh_token or expiry_date at the top level. The next `googleCredentialSchema.parse(credential.key)` in googleAuth then throws.
findings.title: Google refresh stores the safeParse wrapper object as the credential key

findings.consequence: The next `googleCredentialSchema.parse(credential.key)` fails or yields no refresh_token, because the real fields are nested under `data`. Google Calendar integrations break permanently for any user whose token has been refreshed.
findings.explanation: parseRefreshTokenResponse returns the zod SafeParse result, which has the shape {success, data}. It does not return the parsed data. In googleAuth.refreshAccessToken, `const key = parseRefreshTokenResponse(googleCredentials, googleCredentialSchema)` assigns that whole object. It is then written with `prisma.credential.update({data:{key}})`. The old code used `googleCredentialSchema.parse(...)`, which returned the credentials themselves. After the first token refresh the stored key becomes {success:true, data:{access_token, refresh_token, expiry_date, ...}}.
findings.title: Google refresh stores the zod parse result object as the credential key

findings.consequence: This is a behaviour change with a minor effect. Failures now surface as an exception that has less diagnostic information than the old console.error output.
findings.explanation: parseRefreshTokenResponse throws when parsing fails, and on success it always returns success:true. The leftover `tokenResponse.success && tokenResponse.data` is therefore dead code. The change also removed the old error logging for invalid responses. The thrown generic error carries no zod details or response body.
findings.title: Office365 code still checks tokenResponse.success even though the parser throws on failure

findings.consequence: Every SalesforceCalendarService construction rejects its `conn` promise, so Salesforce operations fail. If the import is added, the connection still uses the stale access token.
findings.explanation: The new code calls `prisma.credential.update` at line 96. The file has no `prisma` import; the only match for "prisma" in it is that call. Once the token refresh succeeds, this throws a ReferenceError. Separately, the returned jsforce.Connection is built from `credentialKey.access_token`, the old token, not the freshly refreshed one in `accessTokenParsed.data`.
findings.title: Salesforce getClient uses prisma without importing it, and ignores the refreshed token

prs.title: OAuth credential sync and app integration enhancements

findings.consequence: Permanently unschedulable reminders are reprocessed forever, defeating the retry limit. A single failing DB update in the catch block aborts the whole batch.
findings.explanation: The retry increment only happens inside `if (message?.length && message?.length > 0 && sendTo)`. This is either the `scheduleSMS` falsy-result branch or the catch block. If the message ends up empty (for example a template other than REMINDER with no reminderBody) or `sendTo` is missing (for example `smsReminderNumber` is null), the `if` is skipped and there is no else branch. retryCount stays at 0. The reminder stays `scheduled: false`, so it is selected again on every cron run. The new `retryCount > 1` cleanup therefore never removes it. A second problem is that the catch block's `prisma.workflowReminder.update` is not guarded. If it throws, for example because the row was deleted concurrently or the DB is down, the exception escapes the loop. The handler fails with a 500 and the remaining reminders are not processed. Both updates also write `reminder.retryCount + 1` from the value re…
findings.title: Reminders with empty message or missing sendTo never get retryCount incremented

findings.consequence: Non-SMS reminders with `retryCount` above 1 would be deleted by the SMS cron. Their scheduled sends would be lost without any error.
findings.explanation: The new second branch of the `deleteMany` OR is `{ retryCount: { gt: 1 } }`. It has no `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` filter, so it matches `WorkflowReminder` rows of every method, including email and WhatsApp. The old delete was limited to SMS. This cron endpoint only increments `retryCount` for SMS reminders, so the clause is harmless today. It still turns a cleanup meant for SMS into a table-wide delete. Any other flow that starts using `retryCount` would have its reminders silently deleted here. A related risk is that the `update` inside the `catch` block is not guarded. If the row was deleted concurrently, the update throws and aborts the loop, so the remaining reminders are skipped and the request fails.
findings.title: Retry-exhaustion delete is not limited to SMS reminders

findings.consequence: Non-SMS reminder rows could be deleted by the SMS job if retryCount is ever used for them. SMS reminders are dropped after only two failures.
findings.explanation: The second OR branch of the deleteMany, `retryCount > 1`, has no `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` condition, although this is the SMS cron handler. It deletes any WorkflowReminder row with retryCount above 1, whatever its method. A grep shows only this handler increments retryCount on WorkflowReminder, so other methods stay at the default 0 and are unaffected today. The scoping is still wrong. Any other handler or future code that uses the column would have its reminders deleted by the SMS cron. Because `gt: 1` deletes at 2 failures, the limit is effectively two attempts, and a reminder is removed after a transient Twilio error.
findings.title: retryCount delete branch is not scoped to SMS reminders

prs.title: SMS workflow reminder retry count tracking

findings.consequence: Blacklisted addresses are emailed even though the blacklist exists to prevent that. Existing attendees get a duplicate 'added as guest' email. Mixed-case blacklisted addresses are saved as attendees.
findings.explanation: The handler builds `uniqueGuests` by dropping existing attendees and blacklisted emails. Only `uniqueGuests` is saved to the booking (`guestsFullDetails`). Line 168 then calls `sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests)` with the raw input `guests`. If the input contains an address in BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS, or one that is already an attendee, that address is not added to the booking but still gets the 'guests added' email. The blacklist check at line 77 also compares the guest as typed against lowercased blacklist entries, so `Bad@X.com` passes the filter and is added.
findings.title: Notification emails are sent to the unfiltered guest list, including blacklisted and duplicate guests

findings.consequence: Team admins who are not organizers or attendees are likely refused with FORBIDDEN when adding guests to team bookings. Only users who are both admin and owner pass.
findings.explanation: `isTeamAdminOrOwner` is `isTeamAdmin(...) && isTeamOwner(...)`. The name and intent call for OR. Whether `isTeamAdmin` already counts owners is not shown here, so a plain admin who is not an owner is probably denied. The team query helpers were not checked. When the booking has no team, the check runs against team id 0.
findings.title: Team admin/owner check uses AND instead of OR

prs.title: Add guest management functionality to existing bookings

findings.consequence: After one rejected request, a device over the limit gets anonymous access for the cache TTL of about 29 minutes. Retrying every 29 minutes keeps it in. The enforced device limit can be exceeded in practice.
findings.explanation: The change makes CreateOrUpdateDevice return ErrDeviceLimitReached, and Authenticate rejects the request only when TagDevice returns that error. AnonDeviceService.tagDeviceUI (impl.go:83-95) calls localCache.SetDefault(key) before CreateOrUpdateDevice, and it returns nil on a cache hit. When the limit is reached, a new device is rejected on its first request, but its key stays in the 29-minute cache. Every later request from that device hits the cache, TagDevice returns nil, and Authenticate grants anonymous access without the device ever being stored. The limit therefore only blocks each new device once.
findings.title: Device limit bypassed: rejected device is cached before the store call and then admitted

findings.consequence: The device count can exceed the configured limit under concurrent first requests, and more so with several Grafana instances.
findings.explanation: CreateOrUpdateDevice counts devices and then inserts in separate statements with no transaction or lock. Concurrent requests from different new devices can all see count < limit and all insert.
findings.title: Device limit check is not atomic with the insert

findings.consequence: The anonymous device limit is inconsistently enforced. A rejected device gets anonymous access on its next request, so a client can get past the limit with one retry. Users see intermittent failures: the first request fails and the retry succeeds.
findings.explanation: The change makes TagDevice return the error from tagDeviceUI (impl.go:147). Anonymous.Authenticate in client.go:44-47 now rejects the request when that error is ErrDeviceLimitReached. tagDeviceUI (impl.go:87) writes the device cache key before CreateOrUpdateDevice runs at line 93. When the store returns ErrDeviceLimitReached, the key is already cached. The next request from the same device ID, IP and user agent hits the cache at line 83 and returns nil. TagDevice then returns nil and Authenticate lets the request through. The same device is therefore rejected once, then accepted for the cache TTL of 29 minutes, even though it was never stored.
findings.title: Device-limit rejection is only enforced once per device because the cache is set before the store call

prs.title: Anonymous: Add configurable device limit

findings.consequence: A user can get spurious denials for resources whose name and folder concatenate to the same string as a previously denied pair. Entries live for the short cache TTL.
findings.explanation: userPermDenialCacheKey builds the key as namespace.perm_uid_action_name_parent. Name and parent are joined with "_" and are not escaped. Resource names and folder UIDs can contain underscores. A denial cached for (name "a_b", parent "c") produces the same key as one for (name "a", parent "b_c"). Check short-circuits to Allowed:false on any hit in permDenialCache, before it looks at permissions. A user who was denied one resource can therefore be wrongly denied a different resource they are allowed to access, until the cache entry expires. The key also shares the "perm_<uid>_<action>" prefix with the permission-map key, though the trailing fields keep the two apart. The failure direction is deny, not allow, so this is not an authorization bypass.
findings.title: Denial cache key joins variable fields with "_", so keys can collide

prs.title: AuthZService: improve authz caching
Plugins: Chore: Renamed instrumentation middleware to metrics middleware

findings.consequence: With ad hoc filters set, split queries are sent to Loki with duplicated label matchers or label filters, for example `{a="b", k="v", k="v"}`. This adds redundant work for Loki, and negated or regex filters give the wrong semantics. Interpolated values that contain `$` can be re-interpolated.
findings.explanation: runSplitQuery (querySplitting.ts:296-299) and runShardSplitQuery (shardQuerySplitting.ts:49-52) now call datasource.applyTemplateVariables(query, scopedVars, request.filters) up front. The split code then runs each sub-request through datasource.runQuery (querySplitting.ts:180). That goes through super.query, which calls applyTemplateVariables again with the request's filters. addAdHocFilters/addLabelToQuery does not de-duplicate, so each ad hoc filter is added to the expression a second time. The expression text and the step and legendFormat fields are also run through templateSrv.replace a second time. The old shard code did not pass filters, and the old runSplitQuery did not interpolate at all, so ad hoc filters were applied only once.
findings.title: Queries are interpolated and ad hoc filters added twice in split paths

prs.title: Advanced Query Processing Architecture

findings.consequence: In the list view, users cannot pause or delete Grafana rules from the actions menu. The Silence entry appears but does nothing. Recording rules lose Pause and Export. This is a functional regression with no authorization bypass.
findings.explanation: The change makes AlertRuleMenu compute canPause, canDelete and canSilence from the Grafana prom-rule abilities, so they can be true when rulerRule is undefined, which is the case in the new list view where the ruler request was removed. The rendering code was not updated. The Pause item requires rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule) (lines 123-125), and the Delete item requires rulerRule (line 165). In RuleActionsButtons.V2.tsx the SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer only renders when rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule) is true (line 104), and rule is undefined in the list view. So Pause and Delete never appear in the list. "Silence notifications" is shown because canSilence is true, but clicking it sets showSilenceDrawer and no drawer renders. Separately, the prom ability set gates Pause, Restore, DeletePermanently and ModifyExport on isAlertingRule, whereas the old code allowed any Grafana-…
findings.title: List-view menu grants prom-rule abilities, but Pause/Delete/Silence actions still require a ruler rule

findings.consequence: The UI shows edit and delete actions on federated rules that the ruler API rejects or that should be read-only. This is a regression from the previous behaviour.
findings.explanation: useAllAlertRuleAbilities used to compute isFederated with isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group). The change makes it delegate to useAllRulerRuleAbilities, which hardcodes isFederated = false (the check is commented out as a TODO). A CombinedRule in a federated external ruler group (for example a Mimir federated group) is therefore no longer treated as immutable. Update, Delete, Pause and Restore are now reported as supported where they were NotSupported. isFederatedRuleGroup still exists in utils/rules.ts, and other callers such as RulesGroup and RuleDetailsButtons still use it, so the old behaviour is intended.
findings.title: Federated rule group check dropped from useAllAlertRuleAbilities

findings.consequence: React emits a missing-key warning. Reconciliation of the Grafana rule items is unstable when the filtered list changes or load-more appends, which can cause wrong item reuse and extra re-renders.
findings.explanation: The `key={key}` prop was dropped when GrafanaRuleLoader was replaced by GrafanaRuleListItem in the `rules.map` callback. The other branches (datasource and default) still pass a key.
findings.title: Missing React key on GrafanaRuleListItem in list map

findings.consequence: In the new list view and in the filter view, which now uses GrafanaRuleListItem, the Silence menu item for Grafana alerting rules is shown but does nothing when clicked.
findings.explanation: The change makes `rule` optional, and GrafanaRuleListItem now renders `<RuleActionsButtons promRule={rule} .../>` with no ruler rule. AlertRuleMenu computes `canSilence` from Grafana prom-rule abilities and shows the Silence item, which calls `handleSilence` and sets `showSilenceDrawer` to true. The drawer only renders when `rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule)` is true, and `rule` is undefined in this case, so nothing appears.
findings.title: Silence action does nothing when only promRule is provided

prs.title: Notification Rule Processing Engine

findings.consequence: Storage and legacy error and latency metrics are wrong. Delete metrics get a high-cardinality label, one value per object name.
findings.explanation: When Storage.Create fails (line 45) and when Storage.Update fails, the code calls recordLegacyDuration(true, ...) instead of recordStorageDuration, so a storage failure is counted as a legacy failure. The legacy goroutine in DeleteCollection calls recordStorageDuration (around line 166) instead of recordLegacyDuration. Delete's success path passes `name` as the kind argument (around line 105) instead of options.Kind.
findings.title: Metrics recorded under the wrong storage label or kind

findings.consequence: In mode 3, legacy storage can silently miss creates, updates and deletes. Legacy and unified storage then diverge. The failures only show up as legacy error metrics.
findings.explanation: In Create (line 51), Delete, Update and DeleteCollection, the goroutine builds its timeout context from the caller's request ctx with context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...). The handler returns right after launching the goroutine, and the API server then cancels the request context. The legacy call therefore runs with an already-cancelled or soon-cancelled context. Legacy writes can then fail with context.Canceled, or never run. The goroutines also use obj, objInfo and options after the handler has returned. A detached context is needed, for example context.WithoutCancel(ctx), before applying the timeout.
findings.title: Async legacy writes inherit the request context and are cancelled when the request returns

findings.title: Delete sets the context logger to d.Log instead of the enriched log

findings.consequence: Redundant file I/O and parsing on a cold start under concurrent load. The results are identical, so correctness is not affected. The fix is to re-check the cache after Lock().
findings.explanation: GetWebAssets reads the cache under RLock, releases it, and then takes the write Lock on a miss. It does not check the cache again once it holds the write lock. If N requests arrive while the cache is empty in non-Dev mode, all N see nil. They then take the lock one at a time, and each re-reads assets-manifest.json and overwrites the cache. The exported signature and return type are unchanged, so I found no API compatibility break.
findings.title: No cache re-check after taking the write lock; concurrent cold-start callers each re-read the manifest

findings.consequence: Every SQL expression query is rejected at parse time, even when the sqlExpressions flag is enabled. If the gate were fixed, TablesList and Execute would still fail because the stub backend is unimplemented. Existing SQL expression functionality is lost.
findings.explanation: enableSqlExpressions (pkg/expr/reader.go:194-200) returns false on every path. findings.consequence: Under load at startup, the process can crash with a fatal concurrent map access error. The window is brief but the failure is not recoverable.
findings.explanation: The change adds a call to s.search.TotalDocs() in searchSupport.init, after the goroutine that handles write events has already started. BuildIndex now writes b.cache under cacheMu only around the assignment. TotalDocs ranges over b.cache with no lock. If a write event triggers handleEvent, getOrCreateIndex and BuildIndex while TotalDocs is iterating, the map is read and written concurrently. This can cause a Go "concurrent map iteration and map write" fatal error. The same unlocked iteration also races with concurrent BuildIndex calls from other goroutines.
findings.title: Unlocked b.cache iteration in TotalDocs races with BuildIndex writes from the event goroutine
